title: Why this month's Microsoft patch release is a doozy
gist: Microsoft's September 2026 Patch Tuesday fixed a record ~972 vulnerabilities (112 critical), part of an industry-wide surge in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery that security researchers call the 'new normal,' with debate over whether patch volume is outpacing actual exploit risk.

insights.claim: Microsoft's September 2026 patch release fixed roughly 972 vulnerabilities, 112 of them rated critical severity, with the rest rated important.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Track Microsoft's patch cadence as a leading indicator of how fast AI-assisted vulnerability discovery is scaling industry-wide attack-surface exposure.
insights.locator: Microsoft's patch for September is a doozy

insights.claim: Microsoft's monthly patch counts have been setting records in rapid succession: roughly 570 vulnerabilities two months prior, then about 620 the following month, then ~972 in September.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A steep month-over-month acceleration in patch volume signals rising security-tooling and compliance costs across enterprises running Microsoft software.
insights.locator: It was only two months ago

insights.claim: Microsoft has already fixed 2,760 vulnerabilities in 2026 year-to-date, more than double the total from the prior year, putting it on pace to exceed the combined vulnerability counts of 2023, 2024, and 2025.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A doubling of disclosed vulnerabilities year-over-year implies materially higher patch-management and vulnerability-response headcount/tooling needs for enterprise IT budgets.
insights.locator: Already this year, Microsoft has fixed 2,760

insights.claim: Two weeks before this patch release, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, Google, Microsoft, and roughly 100 other companies and organizations signed an open letter warning that the window for patching vulnerabilities is narrowing ahead of an expected wave of AI-enabled attacks that exploit them first.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A cross-industry coalition explicitly warning about an AI-driven exploit race suggests security vendors and cloud providers expect faster attacker weaponization cycles, a tailwind for patch-management and detection vendors.

themes.theme: AI arms race in vulnerability discovery

insights.claim: Zero Day Initiative researcher Dustin Childs describes the pattern of record-setting monthly patch spikes as the 'new normal,' driven by AI-assisted vulnerability discovery that shows no sign of slowing.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: If AI-assisted bug hunting is structurally raising discovery rates, expect sustained elevated patch cadence across the industry, not a one-off spike.
insights.quote: On the one hand, congrats to the security gnomes at Microsoft for being able to patch bugs at this rate. On the other hand, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery shows no signs of slowing down.

insights.claim: Despite the surge in AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, there has not yet been a corresponding spike in active exploitation of those flaws, according to Dustin Childs.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The absence of exploit spikes so far tempers near-term panic, but the article frames it as a lagging indicator that could still turn, not proof the risk is overstated.
insights.quote: However, we have not seen a correlating spike in active exploits—yet.

insights.claim: Critics of AI-assisted vulnerability hunting question both its cost and false-positive rates, and suspect vendors of using it partly to justify the billions they are spending on building the same AI systems now being marketed for security.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Investors should discount some vendor claims about AI security ROI until independent, longitudinal data separates genuine bug discovery from noise generated to justify AI capex.
insights.locator: The effectiveness of AI-assisted vulnerability hunting

insights.claim: Mozilla reported in May that its researchers, using an AI tool called Mythos, found a record 271 vulnerabilities with almost none being false positives, offered as counter-evidence that AI-assisted bug hunting is genuinely effective rather than just noisy.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A low false-positive rate at Mozilla is an early data point that could support broader enterprise adoption of AI vulnerability-hunting tools if replicated elsewhere.
insights.locator: Mozilla, for instance, said in May

insights.claim: The true long-term effectiveness of AI-assisted bug hunting will not be knowable for at least a year or more, meaning current record patch counts should be read as an early, unproven signal rather than settled evidence either way.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating AI-security vendors should expect a multi-quarter lag before ROI claims can be validated against real-world outcomes.

themes.theme: Notable and dangerous flaws in this release

insights.claim: September's release includes two zero-day vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-81963 in the Windows update service and CVE-2026-85880 in the Windows Advanced Local Procedure, with no public information yet on who is exploiting them or how broadly.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Unattributed active zero-days in core Windows services warrant immediate patch prioritization by enterprise security teams.
insights.locator: Notable vulnerabilities in this month's release

insights.claim: CVE-2026-55007 lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker achieve code execution on an Exchange Server simply by sending an email with a malicious Visio attachment.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A zero-click, unauthenticated RCE in Exchange is a high-value target for ransomware operators and should be a top patch priority for any organization running on-prem Exchange.

insights.claim: One of this month's SQL Server privilege-escalation flaws, CVE-2026-65669, is triggered when a user submits instructions through SQL Copilot, an AI feature.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: An AI-copilot feature itself becoming an exploit vector is an early concrete example of AI assistants expanding rather than shrinking enterprise attack surface.

insights.claim: Dustin Childs found so many wormable vulnerabilities in September's release — flaws that require no user interaction and can spread machine-to-machine — that he stopped counting after reaching 20.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A high count of wormable bugs raises the near-term risk of a fast-spreading, self-propagating outbreak similar in mechanism to past worm incidents.
